title: From Gas Stations to Courtrooms: The Improbable American Life of Butter Chicken and Dal Makhani
excerpt: An Indianapolis food critic finds transcendent dal makhani behind a gas station's pizza warmer — while in Delhi, two restaurant dynasties battle in court over who invented it.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Dal makhani and butter chicken are central to a unique culinary dispute in India.
  • Moti Mahal and Daryaganj both claim to have invented these iconic dishes.
  • Butter chicken is now America's second-most-ordered Indian dish after tikka masala.
  • Dal makhani is popular in both high-end restaurants and casual eateries across America.
  • The lawsuit could award up to $240,000 in damages, highlighting the dishes' cultural significance.
The Great Butter Chicken Debate

At Bombay Karahi in Indianapolis, the dining room is a row of booths tucked behind a gas station's pizza and fried food warmers. The only decor, as IndyStar food critic Liz Biro recently noted, is high-definition photos of sparkling-wet vegetables that almost certainly migrated from a former Subway tenant. The dal makhani, however, is transcendent — a heaping deli container of burnt-orange lentils, flecked with cilantro and crowned with a spiral of cream, served alongside a small boat of basmati rice and $3 garlic naan. This is what Indian food in America increasingly looks like: not a single story of white-tablecloth tasting menus or a single story of strip-mall curry houses, but both at once, often within the same zip code. And at the heart of both ends of the spectrum sits dal makhani and its better-known sibling, butter chicken — two dishes whose improbable journey from post-Partition Delhi to gas-station Indianapolis is now being litigated in a Delhi courtroom. ## The Lawsuit India Is Watching The Delhi High Court is considering one of the most unusual intellectual-property disputes in food history: who invented butter chicken and dal makhani? On one side is Moti Mahal, the storied Old Delhi restaurant founded by Kundan Lal Gujral after Partition in 1947. On the other is Daryaganj, a newer chain started by Kundan Lal Jaggi's grandson — Jaggi being the other Kundan Lal, who was Gujral's co-founder and fellow Peshawar refugee. Both men worked together at a restaurant in Peshawar before Partition forced them across the border. Both helped build Moti Mahal in Delhi's Daryaganj neighborhood. Both families now claim their patriarch alone invented the dishes that would become India's most famous culinary exports. The origin story, as Moti Mahal tells it, is beguilingly practical. Gujral worried about unsold tandoori chicken drying out — refrigeration was scarce in 1940s Delhi. He devised a rich tomato-butter sauce to rehydrate the leftovers. The makhani — literally "buttery" — gravy worked so well that it became a dish in its own right. He applied the same formula to black lentils, and dal makhani was born. Daryaganj's counsel has called Moti Mahal's claims "misconceived and baseless," arguing both founders contributed equally. The case, which could award up to $240,000 in damages, remains unresolved. ## How Dal Makhani Conquered America

While the founders' descendants fight over credit, the dishes themselves have spread far beyond either restaurant. Butter chicken is now America's second-most-ordered Indian dish after tikka masala, according to restaurant data platforms, and dal makhani has become the go-to vegetarian alternative — a creamy, nutty, profoundly comforting dish that translates effortlessly across contexts. That translation has happened in two directions simultaneously. At the high end, chefs like Sujan Sarkar at Indienne in New York and Himanshu Saini at Trèsind in London are deconstructing the makhani tradition — serving smoked chicken makhani under gorgonzola tortellini, or reimagining the butter sauce as a fine-dining component. At the other end, Bombay Karahi and hundreds of gas-station, grocery-store, and tiffin-service operations across the American Midwest and South are serving the dishes in their most accessible form, often for under $10. For NRIs, both versions carry the same emotional payload. The dal makhani at a gas station in Indianapolis and the makhani-sauced course at a $195 tasting menu in Hudson Yards are drawing from the same well — the same post-Partition kitchen, the same yearning for home, the same dish that has fed India's diaspora from Daryaganj to Dallas.
Culinary Evolution of Dal Makhani
›Served in fine dining and casual settings.

## The Dish That Bridges Everything Moti Mahal, now run by Gujral's grandson Monish, operates more than 100 locations worldwide. The lawsuit will eventually determine whether one family can claim the "inventor" trademark. But in American strip malls and gas stations, in fine-dining rooms and family kitchens, the dish itself has moved beyond any single claim of ownership. It belongs to everyone who has ever needed comfort in a deli container, served behind a pizza warmer, ten thousand miles from home.
